meta.description: Walks, patios and pavers in Warren, MI cleaned with a wide, low spray and a plan for where the water goes. Free itemized estimates from HD Landscape.

hero.title: Clean walks, **and a plan for the runoff.**
hero.lede: Warren is mostly hard surface, and everything that goes down a storm drain here ends up in the Red Run. HD Landscape cleans walks, patios and pavers with a wide, low spray, and works out where the water will go before we start.

local.title: In Warren, a wash starts with where the water goes.
local.intro: The city's master plan divided Warren into equal map cells and found 99 percent of them mostly hard surface, and all of the city drains to the Red Run. So the age of the paving matters here, and so does where the rinse water will end up.

points.title: Everything runs to the Red Run
points.body: The master plan puts the whole city in the Red Run subwatershed, and storm drains lead straight to local water. That makes plain water the place to start, and it means working out where the rinse will run ahead of time.

points.title: 1960s concrete, newer pavers
points.body: The median home here dates to 1965, so many walks and patios are likely old poured concrete, sometimes next to pavers added later. They clean differently. Concrete wants steady, even passes. Pavers need the spray kept from running down the joints.

points.title: Tight lots near the south end
points.body: On the smaller lots along the Detroit border, a walk can run right up against a neighbor's drive. The surface should be cleared first and the spray aimed so the grime does not land on the other side of the line.

points.title: Green usually means a wet spot
points.body: The county calls this area one of the most lacking in tree canopy in southeast Michigan, so a walk that goes green here may not be a shade problem. A downspout, a north wall or a low spot can keep it wet just as well. Find what is keeping it damp, because a wash alone will not stop it coming back.

logistics.title: Before the wash, find the low end of the slope.
body: Jake looks at the surface, the joints and the low end of the slope, then writes a free itemized estimate with a straight answer on what will come off. A careful wash tries a small, out of the way spot first, keeps the spray low and steady, and finishes with a clean water rinse.

A clean surface shows any gaps, so that is the time to see whether the joints need a top up or [polymeric sand](/polymeric-sand/). We serve commercial properties too, so if you look after a storefront or office walk on one of the city's main roads, send a photo and ask whether it fits what we do.

faq.q: Do you do pressure washing in Warren?
faq.a: Yes. HD Landscape pressure washes walks, patios and pavers in Warren, and it is a city we work in often. For a driveway or another surface, text a photo to [(586) 718-8762](tel:+15867188762) and Jake can say whether it is one for us.

faq.q: Where does the rinse water go in Warren?
faq.a: Usually down the walk or drive to the street, then into a catch basin. The flyer the city posts from the Clinton River Watershed Council says storm drains lead directly to local water bodies, and it lists soap, cleaning products and soil among the things to keep out. From there it is the Red Run, which is why the slope matters before any water comes out of the wand.

faq.q: I live on a gravel road in Warren. Does that change anything?
faq.a: A little. Your runoff likely heads for the ditch out front, not a catch basin, and the city asks homeowners on gravel roads to keep those ditches clear of leaves and debris. So loose debris should come off the surface first, and the rinse should be aimed with the ditch in mind.

faq.q: Is spring or fall better for pressure washing?
faq.a: Either works, for different reasons. Spring clears the salt and grit winter left, and Warren's winter guide points out that deicers end up in the street drains. Fall takes care of leaf stains, as long as the leaves go in the compost cart or paper bags and not the gutter, which a city ordinance prohibits. Either way, a wash belongs on a day safely above freezing.
